articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'Project Management, Costing and Quality Assurance' (Digest No.109)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management, Costing and Quality Assurance
IEE Colloquium on Project Management, Costing and Quality Assurance
abstract: Prototyping of expert systems provides a means of augmenting the conventional sequential software development life-cycle; it is not a substitute for it. Any prototyping exercise requires a consideration of two levels of system description, namely the prototype system itself and the ultimate desired system whose design alternatives are to be explored by the prototype. Neither system description can be complete in practice since firstly the complete technical description of the ultimate system is impossible without experimentation, and secondly the prototype is an incomplete simulation of the full-scale system. The relationship between the ultimate operational system, sets of prototypes, prototype of prototypes, and so on, need to be managed explicitly in order to ensure that the appropriate conclusions, concerning hardware, software, development methodology are associated with the correct level of specification. The hardware and software tools needed during the prototyping phases of system development, when flexibility of alternative design and implementation is most important, are generally not the same as those required during the design and implementation of the operational system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Quality assurance and expert systems: principles and practice
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management, Costing and Quality Assurance
abstract: The paper concerns expert system quality assurance (QA) both by formal QA procedures and by techniques such as verification and validation. The problems particularly posed by expert system technology include difficulties in establishing correctness, reliability, and specifying and maintaining the software. However, the software engineering discipline has developed many methods to establish quality in these areas. These methods also can be applied to expert systems and their specific problems. Practical aspects of ensuring quality are expressed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Expert systems: quantification of costs and benefits
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management, Costing and Quality Assurance
abstract: Summary form only given. Concerns the most promising ways to put forward and justify expert systems projects. Furthermore, a methodology for delivering applications for competitive advantage is outlined. A proposal for an expert systems development will be judged by management as an investment decision. This means that only the projects where future benefit to the organisation could be measured will be considered. Cost and benefit measures are considered in relation to times, money, opportunity, communication, cost control, staff and organisation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management, Costing and Quality Assurance
abstract: The technology of expert systems and the tools which support it are now sufficient for an immense number of cost-effective, commercially viable systems to be put in place. The management skills involved in the delivery of such systems are not similarly advanced, and are often fragmentary and, in many cases, poor. The paper discusses various management techniques, mostly based on conventional software systems development or common sense. It is suggested that the successful uptake of mainstream expert systems technology depends more on discipline and proper management than on the implementation of leading-edge technology. There is currently a lack of rigour and professional discipline in expert systems management.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Using knowledge-based system kernels to improve quality
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management, Costing and Quality Assurance
abstract: This presentation explores some of the issues involving the use of knowledge-based system kernels and their effect on the implementation of operational systems. With certain provisos and pre-conditions it is argued that such kernels enhance the prospect of delivering a high-quality solution to users.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Configuration management: how it applies to expert systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Project Management, Costing and Quality Assurance
abstract: Configuration management (CM) is a discipline involving implementing (manually or by computer) plans and procedures to keep track of items being developed, so that at any time it is possible to describe the system completely with respect to what it is supposed to do; what it currently does; what items make it up; how to use it; what problems are associated with it; and its history. The basic features of a good CM system are identification of all configuration items by name and by version number: establishment of relationships between items; establishment of baselines and change management; and report and audit of configuration items. The paper examines the application of such techniques in expert system developments.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
